messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The assault occurred on a Tuesday evening in late October. Margaret had stayed late at the courthouse, reviewing discovery for a felony trial set to begin the following week. As she walked through the basement parking garage toward her car, a man came up from behind her, grabbed her arm, and pressed something sharp against her ribs. He took her briefcase — the one her husband had given her for their fortieth anniversary — and shoved her hard against a concrete pillar before running off. She remembered the smell of stale cigarette smoke on his jacket and the way her knees buckled as she slid down the pillar. Security found her twenty minutes later, still sitting on the damp concrete, unable to stand. The man was never identified. The briefcase was never recovered.

Margaret has been a public defender for over forty years. She has represented clients accused of violent crimes, sat across tables from men convicted of assault, and walked through that same parking garage a thousand times. At seventy-eight, she had always thought of herself as someone who could handle whatever came. Her husband, Edward, retired now for a decade, often told her she was tougher than anyone he had ever met.

She frequently looks behind her to check if someone is following her. This is most pronounced in parking garages and courthouse hallways, but it has begun to extend to the grocery store and the sidewalk near her home. She watches other people closely for signs that they might harm her. In the courtroom, her eyes move constantly to the gallery, scanning the faces of family members, observers, and defendants waiting for their cases to be called. She is easily startled. A door slamming, a voice raised in the hallway outside chambers, a hand placed on her shoulder without warning — these cause a physical reaction that leaves her feeling exposed and, she has come to believe, visible in a way that undermines the authority she has spent a lifetime building.

What brought Margaret to seek help was not the symptoms themselves, but a moment in court three weeks ago. She was cross-examining a witness when the bailiff closed a door more firmly than usual. Margaret flinched. The judge paused. The opposing counsel looked up. For the first time in her career, she lost her train of thought in front of a jury. She sat down and could not remember what she had been about to ask. That night, she told Edward she was afraid she was losing her edge. He said nothing for a long time, and then asked if she had ever thought about talking to someone.

Margaret is not certain that talking will help. She has spent her life arguing, questioning, analyzing — she is not sure what it means to sit on the other side of the table. But she is tired of looking over her shoulder. She is tired of the way her heart pounds when a colleague approaches from behind. She is tired of feeling, at seventy-eight, like a woman who cannot trust the world she has navigated for decades. What she fears most is that this will cost her the work she loves. What she hopes, though she would not say it aloud, is that someone can tell her why she cannot shake the sense that someone is always there, just behind her.
